In practical decoy-state quantum key distribution (QKD), an adversary typically substitutes single photons with multi-photon states to execute a single-photon source attack, thereby extracting extra information about the key. This study demonstrates that even if an eavesdropper lacks full knowledge of the users' decoy intensities, they can still conduct successful attacks by targeting users with higher power pulses using a source that generates photons with varying phase phases. By analyzing the mutual information derived from these non-uniformly phased single photons, an eavesdropper gains additional data on the strongest pulses. Consequently, this gained information enhances the ultimate key rate under specific attack conditions. We anticipate these findings will prompt the research community to reassess security parameters for QKD systems employing partial phase randomization.

This study investigates how pretraining corpora affect in-context (IC) learning within large-scale language models (LLMs). Experiments reveal that an LLM's performance on IC tasks is sensitive to the domain of its training data; specifically, an model pretrained on web data performs poorly on scientific tasks unless also exposed to scientific data during training. Furthermore, an model's proficiency in a domain is contingent upon the inclusion of that domain within its dataset. Additionally, we observe that an LLM's ability to generalize to a domain during IC learning is contingent upon the presence of relevant domain knowledge within its training corpus. Finally, we note that an LLM's performance on a task within a domain is contingent upon the inclusion of that domain within its training data.

We investigate the formation and expansion of cold clouds within galaxy clusters using adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) simulations. These studies explore scenarios where clouds possess uniform or stratified internal structures, varying initial temperatures, and different magnetic field configurations. Our findings indicate that while radiative cooling drives the rapid collapse of these clouds, their subsequent evolution is governed by a balance between thermal conduction, magnetic field strength, and gravity. Notably, when conduction is active, it halts further cooling and prevents fragmentation, resulting in more extended cold regions compared to non-conductive cases. Furthermore, we observe that cold clouds with cooler outer layers experience less fragmentation and greater stability than those with uniform composition. Although magnetic fields provide significant support and enhance cloud longevity, they do not avert total dissipation over timescales of several hundred million years. Ultimately, our results suggest that the formation of extensive, stable cold cores necessitates both initial inhomogeneity in temperature and strong magnetic fields.
This paper examines recent experimental results concerning neutral neutral meson mixing, CP violation, and CPT symmetry within the beauty- and charm-systems.

We investigate the four-point amplitudes involving the new bosonic states of hard superstrings, demonstrating that these states exhibit the characteristic features of hard states observed in the supersymmetric theory. Furthermore, by applying supersymmetry arguments, our results enable the derivation of the four-point amplitudes containing two fermionic and two new bosonic external states. Based on these findings, we propose an extended version of Gross's conjecture, which covers all four-point amplitulates at infinite momentum that include an even number of external fermionic states.

The advent of the Internet of Things (IoT) and 5G mobile networks has necessitated a fundamental evolution in how core network management is conceptualized and executed. To support massive IoT deployments and 5G services, self-organized, sustainable networks are required, which in turn rely on advanced self-awareness and self-healing capabilities. This paper examines the core management procedures essential for achieving these autonomous network functions. Furthermore, it outlines the architecture of a self-aware and self-healing network, emphasizing the critical role of blockchain technology in fostering secure, decentralized communication between network entities.

This study introduces a neural speech synthesis system that requires no external resources, utilizing a discrete vocabulary of perceptual acoustic units (AUs) instead of the conventional continuous acoustic models found in neural text-to-speech (TTS). The primary objective is to synthesize high-quality, natural-sounding speech using a minimal AU vocabulary to simplify model architecture. We also propose a straightforward method for determining the AU vocabulary and a basic transcription strategy. The system employs a unidirectional autoregressive model to generate waveforms, with the number of AUs optimized through the balance between synthesis quality and computational efficiency. We evaluate the approach using the AU vocabulary from the TTS-1 model, which consists of approximately 1,000 AUs. This small set is sufficient to cover the majority of phonemes and suprasegmental features. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable quality to best-in-class neural TTS systems, such as Tacotron2 with a vocoder, while significantly reducing training time and inference speed.

Motion planning is a critical challenge in robotics, and recent advances in planning within 2D and 3D environments have primarily focused on planning among polygonal and polyhedral obstacles. However, many practical obstacles are best modeled using smooth curves, such as circles or splines. To address this gap, we introduce a multi-stage optimization framework designed for placing obstacles defined by piecewise smooth curves. At each optimization stage, a branch-and-bound procedure is employed to compute an optimized upper bound on the shortest path length. A key innovation of this work is a data-driven approach that generates a "tight" outer bound for the planning space by approximating the curvature of these smooth obstacles using coupled convex programming constraints. These curvature data are derived from discrete sampled points on the obstacles, and the computational efficiency of the method is validated through various numerical experiments.

We introduce a broad class of quantum resource theories to investigate how physical states transform into one another under freely available operations, with a specific focus on constraints regarding the manipulation of quantum states. Our findings reveal that achievable convertibility between arbitrary quantum states using a specific set of operations is tightly bounded by the distance to the nearest invariant state within that set. These theorems generalize and sharpen previous theorems concerning majorization, thermodynamics governed by the Gibbs ensemble, and more general thermal operations. Furthermore, our results yield new perspectives on the reversibility of state transformations and clarify the distinct distinctions among single-shot operational frameworks.

This study examines the oscillations of a shallow surface fluid contained within a vertical cylinder that undergoes horizontal periodic displacement. The dimensionless governing equations consist of a second-order nonlinear ordinary differential equation coupled with a nonlinear Advection-Dirichlet boundary value problem, a system inspired by prior experiments on "sloshing coffee." Our primary goal is to identify all periodic solutions to this system. Specifically, we demonstrate that when the driving force amplitude is sufficiently small and the driving frequency avoids specific resonance values, a unique periodic solution exists. Furthermore, under additional constraints regarding frequency and amplitude, we prove the existence of two symmetric periodic solutions that involve slight fluid motion; these solutions branch off from the system's equilibrium state corresponding to a fully flat fluid surface.

This study addresses robust learning in a decentralized environment, where agents aim to minimize the expected loss of a perturbed data distribution that remains within a specific radius of a true, unknown distribution. We introduce a new algorithm, DR-DSGD, a variant of Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSSG), designed to resolve this challenge. We establish a theoretical upper bound on the excess risk of DR-DSGD and, through a carefully selected step-size schedule, demonstrate that convergence to near-optimal solutions occurs with high probability. Our experiments, conducted across various image classification tasks, show that DR-DSGD significantly outperforms existing leading methods in both robustness and efficiency.

We employ the hydrodynamic attractor method to investigate the initial conditions and particle generation resulting from high-energy nuclear collisions. Our findings indicate that, for a given final energy density and entropic yield, the attractor approach necessitates an initial energy density substantially lower than that of a free-streaming equilibrium state. Conversely, when the system's evolution is governed by the Milne self-similar attractor, the final state corresponds to a critical freeze-out marked by a divergent entropy per particle. Finally, by integrating these concepts, we propose an initial condition model wherein the energy density follows a free-streaming evolution toward a critical freeze-out, while the temperature tracks the corresponding hydrodynamic attractor curve.

While high-velocity outflows are commonly observed in high-mass star formation, low-velocity outflows remain less frequent. This study investigates whether high-velocity jets can initiate low-velocity outflows by modeling the evolution of high-mass protostellar outflows using the Jet-Driven Outflow (JDO) framework. We examine four JDO simulations, each featuring a distinct mass accretion rate ($\dot{M}$) of $0.01$, $0.05$, $0.1$, and $0.5\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, respectively. Our results reveal that jet-driven outflows are more powerful and expansive than those powered solely by radiation pressure. Furthermore, the jet's contribution to outflow momentum is inversely proportional to the system's accretion rate. In the scenario with the highest accretion rate ($\dot{M} = 0.5\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$), the jet's role in driving outflow momentum drops to merely 10% of the total. We propose that in environments with elevated accretion rates, the intense force of the jets can not only generate more vigorous outflows but also accelerate material to lower speeds more effectively than in low-accretion systems.

This study presents a balanced control approach for constrained nonlinear systems, enabling the simultaneous achievement of safe operation and high performance. This framework extends the concepts of balance control and control barrier functions by introducing a novel Lyapunov-like function to ensure relative degree systems remain within their bounds. By adjusting this function's parameters, operators can optimize performance while guaranteeing safety. Specifically, for systems with relative degree one, balancing control is achieved through parameter tuning that minimizes a performance cost while maintaining safety guarantees.

This study presents a numerical investigation into the resonant dynamics of minor planets within the asteroid belt, focusing on the effects of solar radiation pressure (SRP). We adapt the framework established by Giuliatti Winter et al. (2017), extending the analysis from mean motion resonances (MMR) with Earth to include resonances involving Venus and Mars. Our findings reveal that, similar to the MMR scenario, the inclusion of SRP significantly alters the secular evolution of the test particle's orbital elements. We identify two categories of SRP semi-MMRs: those that merely shift the primary resonances and others that trigger distinct, independent series of these phenomena. We estimate the spatial domains of the resulting resonances and calculate the periods of the corresponding secular resonant cycles.

We introduce an efficient first-principles light-matter tight-binding modeling framework based on the Peierls phase and the Bloch theorem. By demonstrating that the derived light-matter terms in the tight-binding Hamiltonian remain invariant under a gauge transformation of the vector potential, we validate its reliability. This approach has been validated using the Kagome material Fe$_3$Sn$_2$, where we analyze the optical responses of both isolated monolayers and bulk structures. Our findings reveal that circularly polarized light can break time-reversal symmetry, leading to non-zero anomalous Hall conductivity.

This study introduces a novel object representation categorized as semantic keypoints, designed to facilitate both 2D and 3D object pose estimation under category-level constraints. We define these semantic keypoints as a set of part-level features, where each point is paired with a specific label, derived from human annotations. We propose a unified framework capable of performing object pose estimation on both 2D images and 3D point clouds. In the object pose estimation task, the goal involves predicting a single canonical pose and one instance-specific pose for a given category. We evaluate the approach on the Oxford RobotNet and T-SCAN datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in category-level object pose estimation for 3D scenes. Additionally, we extend the methodology to a shape estimation task aimed at recovering an optimal ensemble of shapes. We also address robust 3D shape estimation, designed to identify the optimal shape within an input set of shapes and 3D scenes populated with multiple objects of the same category. Notably, our method requires no task-specific training data. We demonstrate that this representation and estimation strategy hold significant promise for robotics and computer vision applications.

We define confidence regions for a Cauchy distribution based on $n$ independent observations $x_1, \dots, x_n$. The interval is given by
$$ \left[ \bar{x}_c - t_{1-\alpha/2} s_c, \quad \bar{x}_c + t_{1-\alpha/2} s_c \right], $$
where $\bar{x}_c = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{x_i}$ and $s_c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}} \sqrt{ \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \frac{1}{x_i} - \bar{x}_c \right)^2 }$. The coverage probability of this interval is at least $1 - \alpha$. This result generalizes the well-established confidence interval for a normal distribution, which relies on the sample mean and standard estimate of the original data. In contrast, our method applies to the transformed dataset where each Cauchy observation is reciprocated.

Basket trials are increasingly favored in oncology for evaluating single agents across multiple tumor subtypes simultaneously. These trials typically recruit patients with varying disease states, which may exhibit distinct treatment responses. While recent literature has proposed methods to adapt sample sizes basket-wide or within specific subsets, these approaches often rely on the assumption of non-informative prior distributions. Addressing this limitation, this paper introduces a Bayesian framework for sample size determination that allows for informative priors and dynamically adjusts recruitment targets as trial data accumulate. The methodology explicitly accounts for data sharing between groups and is illustrated through a simulation study.

The industry demand for extremely accurate movements has driven significant research into control strategies that surpass existing limits. Building on the Sequential Loop Closing (SLC) concept originally devised for robotics, this approach offers superior transient and steady-state responses by addressing multiple time-scales within separate control channels. However, traditional SLC implementation relies on exact model knowledge, a constraint incompatible with the fluctuating uncertainties encountered in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a High-Precision Motion System-adapted SLC framework powered by Linear Parameter Varying (LPV) techniques. Practical validation through experiments demonstrates the proposed system's ability to track arbitrary trajectories with precise accuracy despite inherent modeling imperfections and time-dependent uncertainty fluctuations.

We introduce PRNet, a self-supervised learning framework designed for rigid registration between partial point clouds. This approach is particularly advantageous in real-world scenarios where complete surface scans are unavailable, often forcing reliance on methods optimized for complete-to-complete registration. While various existing solutions exist, they typically demand manual feature extraction, reliance on full-to-full learning, or dependency on initial approximations. In contrast, PRNet utilizes self-supervised learning to require no manual features and does not require initial guess values. By employing two key mechanisms—first, a co-registration process that aligns partial clouds while enforcing consistency against any existing overlap; second, the computation of pairwise pairwise normal alignments to leverage local geometric cues—it achieves high performance. Experiments demonstrate that it successfully registers challenging real-world datasets even when the input partial clouds are extremely limited to as few as 10% of the original data.

A group $G$ exhibits the property $R_\infty$ if, for any pair of distinct conjugation classes within it, there exists a mapping $\phi$ such that every element of form $\phi(g)$ is conjugate to $g$ via a power of some element $k \in G$. This property also signifies that for any such pair, there exists a mapping $\phi$ where the number of elements not conjugate to their images under $\phi$ is infinite. This paper demonstrates that for any integer $n \ge 2$, property $R_\infty$ holds for any nilpotent quotient of a quotient of a Baumslag-Solair group $G_n$, which is defined as the quotient of the group by its center.

Recent advances in theory and experiments have revealed that the Standard Model (SM) could support a metastable vacuum, implying an inherent instability. Since the Higgs boson's mass sits near the threshold separating a completely stable vacuum from one that is merely stable, exploring parameters beyond the SM (BOS-BSm) that stabilize this vacuum remains a priority. We present a trajectory-basis, forward-optimization-based approach for inversion time-resolved ultrafast experiment data. This methodology is applied to pump-probe absorption spectroscopy, utilizing a trajectory basis derived from spectral manifold theory, where states are eigenstates of the Hamiltonian conditioned on specific values of a continuous parameter. By framing inversion as an optimization problem that minimizes the discrepancy between simulated and experimental results, we achieve significant speedups during computation. Furthermore, because the simulation step employs an explicitly constructed Hamiltonian, the method offers enhanced spectral resolution and robustly handles noise within experimental data. We validate these capabilities through applications to synthetic dataset with added noise, as well as experimental pump-probe absorption studies covering both hole-burning and stimulated Raman spectroscopy.

This brief study calculates longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for $D$ and $D_s$ mesons, as well as their corresponding next-to-leading order corrections, leveraging the Bethe-Salpeter wave function.

This work establishes the Gelfand-Shilov spaces $S_s$ and $S^s$ through the growth behavior of their Fourier transforms and utilizes these characterizations to derive novel, intuitive criteria for the non-triviality of these spaces. Furthermore, by employing these results, we identify sufficient conditions ensuring that certain Toeplitz operators are not zero on the Bergman space of the first quadrant in $\mathbb{C}$.

Segmenting instances in unlabeled medical imaging remains a major hurdle for deep learning, largely due to domain shifts caused by variations in appearance and morphology between training and target domains. While recent progress has been made with self-supervised and semi-supervised learning, these methods typically demand labeled data in the inference domain. This research introduces a novel unsupervised cross-domain instance segmentation framework utilizing a cyclic segmentation generative adversarial network. The method aligns segmentation latent representations across domains by reconstructing images within the segmentation space using a cyclic adversarial training process. Comprehensive evaluations across three datasets—two for training and one for testing—demonstrate that the model effectively handles challenging scenarios, including distinct appearances and structural discrepancies in the target domain. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/CMU-RI-MachineLearning/segmentationGAN.

This study presents an end-to-end framework for anticipating human actions using Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). The method encodes first- and second-person video sequences into continuous features via a Kernelized RNN, which employs the Radial Basis Function kernel to maintain temporal dependencies. The resulting feature streams feed into an action prediction RNN that utilizes time-encoding with the RBF kernel. This hybrid approach allows the system to learn long-term video patterns without requiring manual action labels or predefined motion segments. Experiments conducted on the HMDB51 and UCF101 datasets demonstrate that the proposed technique outperforms prior art, achieving an average accuracy of 54.8% on HMDB51 and 64.1% on UCF101.

The April 12, 1985, superflare on AD Leonis, a young K2-type star, is considered the most powerful stellar flare ever recorded. Although the event was extensively observed by various instruments, including the Einstein Observatory, the physical mechanisms driving it remain unclear. This study employs model atmospheres to simulate the spectral energy distribution of AD Leo during the flare, fitting the resulting spectra to actual spectral energy distribution data. We find that the flare's energy source is located in the photosphere, where temperatures reached approximately 10,000 K, significantly higher than the quiescent state of about 4,000 K. The heated region had an estimated thickness of roughly 100 km, with electron densities around $10^{17} \, \mathrm{cm}^{-3}$. These findings indicate that the flare's heating mechanism was confined to the photosphere and did not significantly impact the chromosphere or corona. Furthermore, comparing the derived density and temperature with those of a solar flare suggests that the physical properties of flares on the Sun and on AD Leo are comparable.

On a nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifold $M$, we demonstrate that every $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton on $M$ remains unique under infinitesimal deformation within the space of all such instantons. Furthermore, we establish a specific necessary and sufficient criterion for these instantons to deform, expressed as a condition on the covariant derivative of the associated self-dual curvature. These findings stem from and extend our generalization of the Drinfeld compactification method for the frame bundle of $M$ to cases involving the frame bundle of the spinor bundle. Finally, we outline several applications of this broader framework.

A $C$-normal weighted composition operator $T_{\psi,\theta}$, denoted as being normal relative to commutation with $C$, is one that commutes with power of unitary operator $U_z$ power. This study explores $C$-normality in $T_{\psi,\theta}$ acting on the Hardy space $H^2$ and establishes that when restricted to $H^2$, a $C$-normal operator $T_{\psi,\theta}$ must be actually normal. The article also provides a full classification of $T_{\psi,\theta}$ on $H^2$ by examining the properties of the underlying pair $(\psi, \theta)$. The analysis extends to the subspace of $H^2$, denoted as $BMOA$, by examining how $BMOA$ functions affect $T_{\psi,\theta}$ and its $C$-normality. The article concludes by offering a comprehensive classification of $BMOA$ functions $\phi$ for which $T_{\psi,\phi}$ remains $C$-normal.

Let $p$ be a prime number. Our findings demonstrate that the count of large $p$-core $p'$-partitions of $n$, denoted $\text{core}_p^+(n)$, grows without bound as $n \to \infty$. Specifically, for any fixed integers $p$ and $k$, the set
$$ \{ n \le N : \text{core}_p^+(n) \ge k \} $$
tends toward infinity with $N$. Our proof leverages the connection between these partition counts and walks of length $n$ originating from $0$ on the additive residue graph of order $p$. We establish a theorem regarding $n$-walks from $0$ to $x$ for this graph, showing that their counts approach infinity in $n$ and exhibit power-law scaling with respect to $n$. This result extends and refines prior findings by Arno, Martin, and Panholzer concerning $n$-walks from $0$ to $0$.

Neural network research has recently introduced new paradigms for representing and processing 3D point clouds, including ShapeNet, which is utilized in this study. However, smoothness remains a persistent challenge for point cloud data. To address this, we introduce ShapeNet Transformation-Specific (TPC) smoothing, a method designed to enhance smoothness while preserving geometric structure. This approach performs smoothing across multiple transformations, including those from ShapeNet, to increase robustness and invariance. Furthermore, we introduce a new metric for assessing smoothness, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of various smoothing techniques. Using this TPC method, we achieve state-of-the-art results on the shape completion, classification, and part segmentation tasks.

This paper introduces and evaluates the performance of distributed medium access control (MAC) protocols—specifically slotted ALOHA and CSMA—within the context of automotive radar networks. Radar systems employ MAC protocols to prevent collisions during ranging, ensuring that all targets are accurately measured. While CSMA is a prevalent choice for wireless networks, its performance in the radar context has not been thoroughly investigated. Consequently, this study analyzes both slotted ALOHA and CSMA specifically for Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar applications and provides a comparative evaluation of their efficacy.

This study examines how spectral dispersion influences the visibility of entangled two-photon absorption (ETA) within Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference experiments. We demonstrate that even a minimal amount of ETA enhances HOM interference, raising questions about the absolute dispersionless requirement for HOM blocking when considering ETA contributions. Additionally, we quantify the improvements achievable with spectral filtering and introduce a scalable framework for modeling dispersion across multiple dimensions. Finally, we outline specific research directions necessary to fully leverage dispersion and Eta phenomena in advanced nonlinear optical experiments.

This paper calculates the $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces $CP(V)$, where $T$ represents either the multiplicative group of rational numbers or rational circle. The computation proceeds by $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology of the associated vector space $CC^\infty(V)$ and applying the axioms of equivariant elliptic cohomohology alongside a crucial short exact sequence. Additionally, we examine how this result relates to Borel reduction and demonstrate that the $T$-equivariant elliptc cohomolog of $CP(V)$ is not isomorphic to the ellipticc cohomolog of the point when considering rational $T$-action.

Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion (TKGC) aims to forecast missing facts within a TKGraph, a network comprising entities, predicates, and temporal features. Existing research on TKGC primarily relies on embedding models that utilize complex, non-linear mechanisms, which often result in excessive computational costs and hinder generalization across different scenarios. This study introduces a straightforward yet efficient framework designed to accelerate TKGC without compromising performance. Our method employs minimal linear embeddings to represent entities, predicates, and time units, subsequently replacing standard high-complexity projections with a unified, flexible representation scheme that handles relations over time. Furthermore, we propose a dual-representation architecture for temporal relations: a relational graph utilizing multi-layer perceptrons to capture inter-relation dependencies, alongside a per-instance reasoning component that adapts specific TKGC models to individual triples. Empirical evaluations on established benchmarks demonstrate that this linear embedding-driven approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods while delivering significantly faster execution speeds.

In this study, we investigate the influence of ground sound on Rayleigh waves, focusing specifically on their dispersion characteristics. Our numerical simulations examine various ground models, ranging from homogeneous and heterogeneous media to those exhibiting random heterogeneities. Numerical findings are contrasted with analytical results derived from a 1-D WKB approximation. Additionally, we propose an analytical method for determining the effective (average) wave velocity in heterogeneous ground models, ultimately discussing how these ground characteristics impact the detectability of low-frequency signals.

The standard demonstration of quantum entanglement without invoking inequalities, exemplified by the "all-versus-nothing" proof of Bell nonlocality, relies on the rare condition where measurement outcomes are perfectly correlated. This study investigates a "non-locality without inequalities, without perfect correlations" phenomenon in a system of two observers measuring entangled states that exhibit only non-perfect correlations. Our findings reveal that while optimal local operations cannot produce perfect correlations, sub-optimal strategies can generate them, thereby establishing an interdependence between the optimal extractable entanglement and the existence of perfect correlations. Consequently, this relationship offers a novel perspective on entanglement resources.

Flat bands refer to flat energy spectra, implying zero curvature, which causes associated wave functions to remain eigenstates under any time evolution. These bands are typically linked to flatter spectral regions, often resulting from strong disorder or specific symmetries that restrict electronic states to be either localized or delocalized. In this study, we examine flat band systems by revising the conventional definition of flat bands and investigating the impact of flat bands on the mobility of quasi-two-dimensional systems. We demonstrate that flat bands inherently produce states with extremely low mobility, effectively behaving as localized states. Furthermore, we show that flat bands generate singularities in the density of states (DOS), a phenomenon that can be quantified by calculating the minimum spreading of wave packets. In conclusion, we argue that flat band singularities in the DOS are sufficient to localize electronic states, even in the absence of disorder-induced localization mechanisms.

The recent experimental findings of superconductivity in hydrogen boride ($\text{H}_3\text{B}$) at 140 K, a record-breaking temperature within hydrogen-rich compounds, sparked significant interest. In this study, we conducted a systematic first-principles investigation of superconducting properties in $\text{text{H}_3\text{B}}$, utilizing the conventional electron-phonon coupling framework. Our calculations reveal that electron-phonon interactions are notably weak, yielding a modest superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$) of approximately 10 K, which starkly contrasts with experimental reports exceeding 100 K. We propose that achieving such ultra-high $T_c$ values in hydrogen boride requires a mechanism beyond standard electron-phonon coupling, potentially aligning with recent theoretical suggestions of electron-electron interactions mediated by magnetic fluctuations.

When flattening a random partition of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, we denote the count of elements appearing in parts of cardinality $k$ as $R_k$. As $n$ grows toward infinity, the joint distribution of these run lengths $R_1, R_2, \dots$ converges to a specific limiting model. This same distribution arises in two other distinct scenarios: flattening a uniformly chosen partition of an integer chosen from a Geometric$(1/e)$ distribution, and modeling the number of visits to state $k$ by a continuous-time Markov chain that transitions from state 1 to infinity with state-dependent rates $u_k = k! e^{-e^{-xt}}$. Furthermore, we examine the case where partitions are conditioned on having exactly $k$ parts.

This study investigates amenability within arithmetic groups, focusing on two core concepts: stiffness and charmability. While the STVVV theorem (or similar variant) establishes that the stiffness of such groups correlates with the solvability of their congruence subgroups, we expand this exploration by examining several pertinent arithmetic groups, including the $4\times 4$ special linear group over the rational integers.

Fail-operational systems are essential in safety-critical fields, enabling continued system functionality after a failure. Achieving this state requires deploying redundant subsystems alongside sophisticated failure management strategies. Due to the escalating complexity inherent in modern redundant architectures, there is a pressing need for formal methods to verify these systems rigorously. This paper presents the formal verification of a driving system utilizing a fail-operational redundancy design. By employing model checking, we automatically demonstrated the capability to maintain safe driving operations following various component and subsystem malfunctions.

We introduce a novel data-driven clustering approach for dynamical systems that relies on distance metrics to evaluate system similarity. The system-wide influence on every other system is captured by the $\mathcal{C}^0$ norm of their Green-Gram operator, which serves this distance as provided theoretical theorems demonstrate their equivalence to the Hausdorff distance between ranges spaces. The existing literature provides proofs of these distances' properties, which we then apply to a data-driven context supported by an offline algorithm capable of processing time-series information. The methodology was validated on both synthetic datasets and real-world data from the Human Activity Perception (HAP) system.

This study examines contemporary research on reconstruct Leibnizian calculus procedures, with a focus on two primary issues: the handling of infinitesimals and the sourcing of foundational principles. We analyze three dominant approaches—namely, Robinson's nonstandard analysis, Lawvere's hyperreal topos, and Kelp's Leibnizian conditional standard part rule—evaluating their specific strategies regarding infinitesimals and axiomatic sources. Our discussion concludes with a critique of these reconstructions and outlines prospective research avenues.

Using the EPT1 interferometric array, HI intensity mapping will observe the large-scale structure of the universe at redshifts between 0.4 and 2.5. Predictions from first-order perturbation theory are generated to assist in calibrating these observations and eliminating foregrounds. The study demonstrates that the nonlinear term significantly impacts the bispectrum, particularly at low $k$ values, and that perturbation theory accurately forecasts the skewness. The bispectrum forecast shows a roughly 10% reduction in signal-to-noise ratio after applying foreground removal, whereas the power spectrum remains largely unaffected. The observed skewness is predicted with negligible error, and the results indicate that intensity mapping using EPT1 could potentially measure cosmic shear.

In the context of vector spaces, operator independence constitutes a distinct concept from vector independence. For instance, consider linear operators acting on a vector space $V$ with a countably infinite basis; these operators can be entirely independent despite not forming independent vectors themselves. Conversely, there exist sets of independent vectors that do not correspond to independent operators. This paper establishes that any collection of dimensionally infinite vector spaces, each possessing a countably infinite basis and spanning a space with dimension at least two, admits a set of $2^{\aleph_0}$ pairwise commuting, algebraically, and multiplicatively independent (along with left-independence) operators over a ground field that also exhibits independence to the right. Our construction yields linear operators characterized by exceptional regularity, specifically exhibiting a minimal number of exceptional values and containing no constants or solely monomials as exceptional terms.

Hybrid recommender systems are increasingly favored over other approaches for their robustness and superior accuracy. This paper introduces a novel hybrid model designed to enhance the performance of user-based collaborative filtering. By incorporating the document contexts of users into the algorithm, we achieve more precise recommendations, effectively mitigating sparsity issues often found in traditional user-based collaborative filtering. We evaluate the proposed system using the MovieLens 1M dataset, comparing it against standalone methods: document-based collaborative filtering, item-based collaborative filtering, and various hybrid systems. Results indicate that our new algorithm outperforms all these benchmarks in accuracy.

This review examines noncommutative probability from a random matrix perspective, with a primary focus on conditions leading to freeness and a specific variant known as conditional freeness. It begins by outlining the fundamental definitions of these concepts alongside key findings. It then explores two major scenarios: first, analyzing independence and freedom among random unitary or orthogonal matrices; second, investigating freedom and conditional freedom involving self-adjoint Hermitian matrices equipped with invariant measures. A final section outlines open questions within this field of study.

This study revisits the monitoring of real-time systems for properties defined over infinite behaviors, expanding the existing framework by introducing two key enhancements. Initially, it generalizes input handling by accommodating both discrete data points and continuous streams, a capability demonstrated through an application to timing constraints within property definitions. Secondly, it introduces a flexible hierarchy of granularity for the continuous streams themselves. This approach enables a trade-off between the precision of virtual time approximation and system runtime overhead, allowing monitors to either approximate or exactly compute based on specific granularities. By leveraging morphisms between approximation levels, a single universal monitor is constructed and shown to be applicable across different granularities.

The LHCb collaboration recently documented the $\bar{B}_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar{B}_s^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980)$ decay processes, which exhibit comparable rates. This study investigates the underlying mechanism of these transitions, specifically the mixing between the $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ resonances, by analyzing angular distributions. We find that the final state $J/\psi f_0(980)$ can be generated through the intermediate $J/\psi f^0(980)$ channel, where $f^0(980)$ represents a scalar isoscalar resonance. Conversely, producing a final state of $J/\psi a_0(980)$ via the direct $\bar{B}_s^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980)$ pathway is prohibited by isospin symmetry. Consequently, the observation of $\bar{B}_s^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980)$ must result from mixing between the $a_0(980)$ and the $f^0(980)$ resonances. The GRAVITY instrument at the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) combines four beam combiners to deliver both polarimetric and high-precision astimetric capabilities. Its acquisition camera (AC) is a critical subsystem designed to automatically determine the image of a star at the focal plane, ensuring optimal alignment for interferometry by maximizing coherence. This camera operates by projecting the incoming stellar light onto a 2048 × 2048 pixel EMCCD detector via a 4f optical setup that mirrors the coherence plane. Functioning as an essential auto-guidance tool, the AC supports both manual and automatic operations. While manual mode allows a user-defined region of interest (ROI) to be selected for interferometry, automatic mode utilizes a variant of the cross-correlation maximum likelihood algorithm to precisely centroid stars within a defined ROI. Testing in automatic mode has demonstrated an accuracy of approximately 0.001 pixels for single stars brighter than magnitude 8, improving to roughly 0.0005 pixels for objects brighter than magnitude 6.

The generalized $k$-center problem involves selecting a subset of $k$ cluster centers from a given set of $n$ points to minimize the maximum distance required to connect every point in the set to its nearest selected center. In this work, we examine this problem through the lenses of Doubling Dimension and Highway Dimension. For instances with low highway dimension, we present an $O(\log^2 n)$-approximation algorithm, which improves upon the previously best-known bound of $O(\log n \cdot \alpha)$ (where $\alpha$ represents the aspect ratio). Additionally, we establish an $\Omega(\log n)$ lower bound for this problem when parameterized by highway dimension, implying that a polynomial-time approximation scheme with approximation factors sublinear in $\log n$ is unlikely. In contrast to these positive results regarding highway dimension, we demonstrate that general $k$-center instances can exhibit arbitrarily large doubling dimension even within grids. Consequently, we prove that any approximation algorithm achieving a factor better than $O(\log n)$ for the generalized $k$-center problem would be impossible for certain grid instances.

This paper focuses on solving multivariate polynomial systems with real coefficients, addressing scenarios involving both coefficient perturbations and arbitrary solution multiplicity. Leveraging existing literature, we establish novel upper bounds for the number of sign evaluations required to locate all isolated roots, surpassing current estimates in cases of high multiplicity. Furthermore, we introduce a new bound that improves upon previous limits for systems featuring low degree or a small count of variables. To enhance computational efficiency, we suggest and evaluate an early termination strategy applicable to any Groebner-basis-based solver.

In photonic systems with parity symmetry, two distinct types of unidirectional sources exist: parity-induced emitters (P-Es) and chiral emitters (C-Es). While C-Es have been thoroughly investigated, P-Es remain underexplored. This study introduces the concept of balanced dual-directional directionality, termed Parity-Symmetry Protected Bundle Emission (PSBE), realized through P-Es. We demonstrate that P-Es function as single-emission bundles directed toward both left and right, where left-right symmetry ensures unidirectional emission within their respective directions. Further analysis reveals that PSBE emerges when multiple P-Es are arranged in alternating patterns, resulting in parallel bundle emissions from adjacent pairs that travel in opposite directions without mutual interference. Consequently, these stable bundles maintain a persistent, parity-protected unidirectional character. We validate these findings using a one-dimensional coupled-resonator system, employing both theoretical modeling and numerical simulations. The proposed P-E based PSBE offers a novel mechanism for generating robust, parity-symmetric unidirectional light sources, complementing existing chiral-based approaches.

We introduce a new, simple, and accurate analytical model describing the thermodynamic equilibrium of alkali metals. Unlike previous approaches that relied on approximations due to the complex structure of their energy levels, our method addresses this complexity without such limitations. This study demonstrates that our model yields precise results for both the Saha ionization degree and the thermodynamic equation of state.

This study investigates the spectral properties of vector mesons within a medium characterized by spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking and chiral imbalance. We employ the Holographic Dual model, utilizing the AdS5 black hole metric modified by a non-trivial profile for the quark mass function to represent the medium. Our in-medium analysis reveals that while the quantum numbers dictate the general behavior of vector mesons, both the temperature and chemical potential influence their masses and widths. Furthermore, we observe that the medium induces a shift in the vector mesons mass spectrum compared to its vacuum state.

Accurately determining the node count in an ad-hoc network is essential for various networking applications. In the Byzantine setting, this task becomes more complex as some nodes may act maliciously, attempting to inflate the reported size. We present novel algorithms for byzantine fault-tolerent network size estimation within small-world networks, surpassing prior results from large-scale environments. Our method leverages encounter-based position trackers to build a virtual network structure, then applies efficient consensus protocols on its properties to derive the final estimate. These approaches achieve higher accuracy than earlier techniques, even when compromised nodes disseminate false information.

Numerical relativity simulations of binary black hole mergers require solving the Einstein field equations, beginning with the generation of initial data that satisfies both the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints. This paper introduces a novel method for deriving these constraints, labeled the Conjugate Gradient Time-Knowledge (CTTK) method. It merges concepts from the conjugate gradient algorithm with the recently developed BSSN (shifting to first order) formalism. Numerical experiments demonstrate that CTTK yields accurate results comparable to established techniques like pseudo-spectral methods and finite elements.

The principal objective of the JUNO project is to determine neutrino mass parameters, achievable through a high-precision measurement of the spectral oscillation minimum. Achieving this requires JUNO's photodetector array to maintain an energy resolution of no worse than 3% at the MeV scale, a standard met by employing over 76,000 large-area photomultiplier tubes (PMTs). These 20-inch reinforced multi-alloy glass PMTs, designed for robust position sensitivity, operate in pairs of various sizes totaling 1,280 units across the water tank. To ensure optical consistency and homogeneity essential for oscillation analysis, a rigorous quality assurance protocol was established. This involves comprehensive testing of every PMT at the optical level, utilizing a dedicated testing rig equipped with a laser source and a CCD camera. This system captures light emission profiles to assess performance characteristics such as gain, spectral response, and position dependence. Results from these tests are analyzed to confirm the mutual optical consistency between matched PMT pairs and to validate overall array consistency. This report details the testing methodology and presents the mass test outcomes for all JUNO PMT units.

Graph-based deep learning models have proven effective in handling complex series prediction tasks, yet their application to multidimensional time series remains limited. This research introduces a novel Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network (AGCN) framework designed to capture long-term dependencies and nonlinear patterns within multidimensional time series data. The model dynamically learns an optimal graph structure, including node weights and edge configurations, to maximize performance. Additionally, a novel loss function has been developed to address data sparsity and imbalance issues. Experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms.

Atmospheric dispersion (atmospheric chromatic refraction) is a wavelength-dependent atmospheric effect that causes light from celestial objects to shift position depending on the object's altitude. For instruments with high spectral resolution, correcting this phenomenon is essential. To characterize dispersion models and evaluate their accuracy, we developed a new methodology utilizing on-sky observations of stars. This technique measures the apparent stellar positions to determine the wavelength-dependent apparent shift, thereby deriving atmospheric models from these apparent positions. To test our approach, we analyzed data from 1000 measurements of 100 stars collected by the 1.2-meter telescope at ESO's La Silla observatory. Our findings indicate that the methodology is robust and capable of precisely measuring atmospheric dispersion with a high level of accuracy.

Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have achieved remarkable success across numerous NLP tasks, yet their massive scale and complex architectures necessitate substantial computational resources for training and inference. Knowledge distillation (KD) offers an effective solution by training a compact student network to emulate a larger ensemble of teachers, thereby reducing costs while often enhancing performance. Standard KL-distance based loss functions for KD, however, often yield suboptimal results when applied to multi-teacher scenarios because they fail to capture critical features of teacher logits. This paper introduces Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), a novel distillation loss that refines student learning through pairwise comparisons involving the input and multiple teachers. Specifically, PILE iteratively ensembles logits from all teachers in every pairwise interaction, enabling the student to acquire richer knowledge from the teachers collectively. Empirical evaluations on various task benchmarks demonstrate that the student model trained with PILE consistently surpasses existing state-of-the-art distillation methods.

Ultralight bosonic dark matter (UBDM) can be represented as a classical wave with an amplitude that fluctuates slowly over time. These fluctuations consist of a primary oscillation set by the particle's mass, combined with secondary terms driven by momentum variations. Our analysis demonstrates that UBDM fluctuations can be sensed through intensity interferometry, a technique relying on measuring fluctuating correlations of intensities between two separated detectors. Unlike standard intensity interferometry focused on spatial correlations, we examine variations at a fixed baseline to derive constraints on UBDM properties. Previous studies have shown spatial intensity correlations vanish for relativistic particles; however, we find that temporally fluctuating correlations persist for non-relativistic UBDM. Specifically, the fluctuating correlation depends on the joint probability distribution of the momenta of the detected UBDM quanta. By applying this insight to an intensity interferometer, one can recover the UBDM mass distribution, offering complementary avenues for detection.
